picks.title: Students Prefer Assistants That Forget
picks.why: Student attitudes to course assistants that remember them.
picks.summary: In a survey of 2,300 undergraduates, 61% preferred a course assistant that kept no memory of them between sessions, mainly for privacy.

picks.title: Hierarchical Summaries Keep Agents on Task for 500 Steps
picks.why: A summarisation scheme that holds up over very long agent tasks.
picks.summary: Agents that summarise every 20 steps into a tree of summaries completed 500-step tasks 2.4 times as often as agents with a sliding window.

picks.title: Rubric-Grounded AI Feedback on Lab Reports
picks.why: AI feedback tied to the instructor's rubric in a university lab course.
picks.summary: Feedback that quoted the rubric criterion it addressed was rated more useful by 540 chemistry students and was contested half as often as free-form feedback.

picks.title: Semester-Long Memory for Course Assistants
picks.why: Per-student memory deployed in university courses for a full semester.
picks.summary: An assistant with per-student session summaries resolved 18% more follow-up questions without a TA, though some students found its recall of past mistakes uncomfortable.

picks.title: Trust Calibration Cues in Code Assistants
picks.why: Which cues help developers reject wrong AI suggestions.
picks.summary: Highlighting uncertain tokens cut acceptance of wrong code suggestions by 27% among 96 developers; confidence scores had no effect.

picks.title: When Students Overrule the Grader: Contesting AI Feedback on Essays
picks.why: How students push back on AI essay feedback.
picks.summary: Undergraduates contested 14% of AI feedback comments and instructors upheld 58% of contests; students who contested revised more.

picks.title: Compress, Then Forget: Budgeted Context for Long-Horizon Agents
picks.why: A learned policy for what an agent keeps, compresses or drops.
picks.summary: A small scorer choosing what to keep verbatim, compress or drop matched full-context accuracy at 35% of the tokens on three agent benchmarks.

picks.title: Retrieval Over Lecture Transcripts Beats Longer Context for Course Q&A
picks.why: Retrieval against long context for a course assistant, with cost.
picks.summary: Retrieving 8 transcript passages answered 9 points more student questions than a 1M-token context, at a fiftieth of the cost.

picks.title: Explanations Increase Over-Reliance on Wrong AI Grades
picks.why: TAs reviewing AI grades trusted wrong ones more when given explanations.
picks.summary: Teaching assistants accepted 31% more wrong AI grades when each grade came with an explanation than when it came alone.

picks.title: Office Hours with an Agent: Who Shows Up?
picks.why: Which students use an AI agent instead of office hours.
picks.summary: First-generation students used an office-hours agent three times as often as human office hours, without dropping human visits.

picks.title: Bird Song Dialects Shift Within a Decade of Urban Noise
picks.why: Self-supervised audio turning volunteer recordings into a decade-long measurement.
picks.summary: A self-supervised audio model over 40,000 recordings showed urban great tits raised their minimum song pitch by 220 Hz in ten years.

picks.title: Context Rot: Agent Accuracy Falls with Session Length, Not Token Count
picks.why: Turn count, not token count, degrades agent context.
picks.summary: With tokens held fixed, agent accuracy fell 2 points per 10 turns, faster when earlier turns held corrected mistakes; pruning those turns recovered most of it.

picks.title: Users Edit Agent Plans More Than Agent Outputs
picks.why: Where people intervene in agent work.
picks.summary: Knowledge workers edited agent plans in 64% of tasks and final outputs in 12%; plan edits halved output correction time.

picks.title: Generative AI Policies Across 120 University Syllabi
picks.why: What instructors allow, ban or require.
picks.summary: Of 120 syllabi, 41% banned generative AI, 37% allowed it with disclosure and 22% required it; requiring courses more often moved assessment in class.

picks.title: Selective Memory Deletion Restores Student Trust in Tutors
picks.why: Letting students control what a tutor remembers.
picks.summary: Giving 300 students a view of and a delete button for their tutor's memory raised trust ratings to the level of a memoryless tutor while keeping the memory's accuracy gains.
